title: The Zoom Cycle
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson argues that detail-oriented people can become so absorbed in improving individual tasks that they lose sight of what their work as a whole is becoming. Writing from a period of rebuilding his career after fourteen years teaching in Indonesia, he observes that his problem was not productivity but deciding which tasks deserved to exist at all. He proposes the Zoom Cycle: zoom out to choose a direction, zoom in to do the work, then zoom out again once reality has supplied evidence. Hutson connects this loop to his CARE Method (Clarify, Articulate, Refine, Execute), stressing that execution feeds back into clarification and that a learning 'destination' should be a compass rather than a contract. He extends the idea to schooling, suggesting that students complete many individual tasks without seeing what larger capacities they are building, which may be why so much school learning evaporates. He also warns that big-picture thinking can become its own form of avoidance, concluding that clarity is often produced by action. The public portion of the post is complete; a paid section adds a practical reset exercise. Filed in Leadership as a close call because its dominant focus is self-direction and decision-making, with education as one application.
points: Hutson reframes feeling busy but directionless as a prioritization problem, not a productivity problem: the question is which tasks deserve to exist.
The Zoom Cycle alternates between choosing a direction and doing concrete work, because living only in details or only in vision both fail.
His CARE Method treats Execute as a feedback point that sends the learner back to Clarify, making learning and planning iterative loops.
Students often master isolated assignments without seeing the larger capacities they serve, which he suggests helps explain why school learning fades.
Big-picture planning can become a sophisticated way to avoid work, so ideas must be tested against reality, since clarity is often produced by action.
quotes: But there is a weakness hidden inside that strength. If you are naturally good at looking closely, you can become so absorbed in improving individual parts of something that you forget to ask what the whole thing is becoming.

That was when I started realizing that productivity was not really the problem. I did not necessarily need another way to organize tasks. I needed a better way to decide which tasks deserved to exist in the first place.
In fact, being productive can sometimes make this harder to notice because there is always evidence that you are accomplishing something. The day feels full. Things get finished.

If you never zoom out, you can spend years becoming efficient at things that are not taking you where you want to go. But if you spend all of your time zoomed out, you can become the person with a beautiful vision, an elaborate five-year plan, and remarkably little evidence that any of it has survived contact with reality.

That is also why I have become so interested in the idea of giving learning a destination. In the CARE Note-taking Method, I wrote that a learner can name a possible destination without pretending to know exactly where an idea will end up. The destination is meant to function as a compass rather than a contract.

When students understand that larger purpose, the smaller activity suddenly has somewhere to go. And perhaps that is one of the reasons so much learning disappears when school ends. Students become very good at completing individual trees without ever being shown the forest.
Big-picture thinking can become another sophisticated way of avoiding the work.
Clarity does not always come before action. Sometimes clarity is produced by action.
